t: Smallest Index With Equal Value — Early-Exit Linear Scan
o: Given a 0-indexed array nums, find the smallest index i where i % 10 equals nums[i], or return -1 if no index qualifies. Example 1 [0,1,2] matches at every index, so the answer is the first one, 0. Example 2 [4,3,2,1]: index 2 is the only position with 2 % 10 == nums[2]; indices 0, 1, 3 fail, giving 2. Example 3 [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,0] never satisfies the condition, so -1. Constraints are tiny (n <= 100, values 0..9), so there is nothing to optimize beyond a clean scan: checking indices in increasing order and returning at the FIRST hit provably yields the minimum, because any earlier index would already have been tested and rejected.
k: Scanning ascending and returning immediately gives the smallest matching index — collecting all matches is unnecessary.
Only the last digit matters: i % 10 cycles through 0..9, which always covers the value range of nums[i].
A full scan is also a lower bound: without inspecting every element you cannot safely conclude -1.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Forward Pass with Early Exit
a.i: Iterate i from 0 upward, compare i % 10 against nums[i], and return the first index that matches. If the loop finishes without a match, no index works and the answer is -1.
s: Iterate i from 0 to n - 1 in increasing order.
Return i immediately on the first success.
a.t: O(n) — one comparison per element with an early exit on the first match.

w: Treat this as a warm-up: state the early-exit invariant (first hit while scanning ascending is the global minimum) and nail the mod-10 detail. Pitfalls: scanning right-to-left (returns the LARGEST index), writing i % len(nums) instead of i % 10, and forgetting the -1 fallback. Edge cases: single-element arrays ([5] fails since 0 % 10 = 0 != 5; [0] succeeds), arrays whose only match sits at the last index. Follow-up: answer many queries 'smallest matching index >= l' by precomputing, for each residue digit, the sorted list of indices holding that digit and binary searching.
